episode_title: Why Do I Feel Guilty Asking for Help? | Ashley Chang Dawson

real_qa.q: What is Sundays and what problem does it solve for working parents?
real_qa.r: Sundays is an executive assistant service for working parents designed to erase the motherhood penalty—how moms and parents are held back from career opportunities and raises. The service employs a team of executive assistants who are themselves moms and caregivers, and they work one-on-one with clients to provide holistic support across both work and home domains, helping ambitious parents reclaim time and energy for what matters most to them.
real_qa.requete: What does Sundays executive assistant service do

real_qa.q: What is the biggest barrier preventing people from using Sundays support services?
real_qa.r: The first barrier is simply allowing yourself to feel like you deserve help. Many people work hard but feel they haven't done enough or haven't accomplished enough on their own before they can justify accepting support. People often set arbitrary definitions of what milestones they need to hit before deserving help, but you don't actually know what it will take to reach those points before you get there. Additionally, people tie their sense of self to their activity and responsiveness, creating a nervous system attachment to being the fastest to respond and the first to see everything.
real_qa.requete: Why do people struggle to ask for executive assistant help

real_qa.q: How does delegating work affect the nervous system and sense of identity in high-performers?
real_qa.r: When you hand off tasks to someone else, your body may resist even though intellectually you want the relief. Ashley recently muted a Slack channel she used to check every morning after delegating those responsibilities. It took her a couple of weeks to separate her identity from the constant hypervigilance and high alert state. She had to allow herself to trust that her team would tell her if something bad happened, rather than needing to be on high alert all the time—this required rewiring her nervous system's attachment to being the person who sees everything first.
real_qa.requete: How does handing off tasks affect your nervous system

real_qa.q: What happens to people's productivity and choices after they gain back time through delegated support?
real_qa.r: Often people take two paths: either they take on more work or commitments because having time feels like they should be doing something else, or they realize they can have a business or role that supports their family without needing more money or constant growth. When they sit with the discomfort of having more time, they can figure out how they actually want to spend it—sometimes choosing time with their kids or rest instead of automatically filling the space with more work.
real_qa.requete: What do people do with freed-up time from delegating

real_qa.q: How has Ashley Chang's relationship with receiving help evolved as Sundays grew from startup to established business?
real_qa.r: In the first phase of Sundays, which is now about three and a half years old, Ashley didn't get any help herself—she was the help, serving as the executive assistant for clients while trying to build the business. She set a milestone of needing to make enough money to pay herself before she could reasonably pay someone else. While this was initially sustainable and exciting, it slowly ate away at her energy until she became exhausted every day, showing her the model wasn't sustainable long-term.
real_qa.requete: When did Sundays founder start receiving help herself

guest.bio_context: Ashley Chang spent years working in fast-moving, high-performance tech environments in the San Francisco area, primarily in technical roles leading engineering teams and defining product strategy. She worked predominantly in male-dominated tech spaces where she was often the only woman or one of few women in the room. Before founding Sundays, she actively mentored women and worked to increase female representation in tech.
